'''''Banksia integrifolia''''', commonly known as the '''coast banksia''',<ref name="PLANTNET">{{cite web |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Banksia~integrifolia |title=PlantNET - FloraOnline |author1=Harden, G.J. |author1-link=Gwen Harden |year= |website=PlantNET (The NSW Plant Information Network System) |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens and Domain Trust, Sydney |access-date=25 May 2024}}</ref> is a [[species]] of [[tree]] that grows along the east coast of [[Australia]]. One of the most widely distributed ''[[Banksia]]'' species, it occurs between [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] and [[Central Queensland]] in a broad range of [[habitat (ecology)|habitats]], from coastal [[dune]]s to [[Great Dividing Range|mountains]]. It is highly variable in form, but is most often encountered as a tree up to {{convert|25|m|ft}} in height. Its [[leaf|leaves]] have dark green upper surfaces and white undersides, a contrast that can be striking on windy days.

It is one of the four original ''Banksia'' species collected by [[Joseph Banks|Sir Joseph Banks]] in 1770, and one of four species published in 1782 as part of [[Carolus Linnaeus the Younger]]'s original description of the genus. It has had a complicated [[taxonomy (biology)|taxonomic]] history, with numerous species and varieties ascribed to it, only to be rejected or promoted to separate species. Modern taxonomy recognises three [[subspecies]]: [[Banksia integrifolia subsp. integrifolia|''B. integrifolia'' subsp. ''integrifolia'']], [[Banksia integrifolia subsp. compar|''B. integrifolia'' subsp. ''compar'']] and [[Banksia integrifolia subsp. monticola|''B. integrifolia'' subsp. ''monticola'']].

A hardy and versatile [[garden plant]], ''B. integrifolia'' is widely planted in Australian gardens. It is a popular choice for parks and streetscapes, and has been used for bush [[revegetation]] and stabilisation of dunes. Its hardiness has prompted research into its suitability for use as a [[rootstock]] in the [[cut flower trade]], but has also caused concerns about its potential to become a [[weed]] outside its natural habitat.

== Names ==
Now widely known as the '''coast banksia''' or '''coastal banksia''', ''B. integrifolia'' was previously known by a range of common names. The ''Checklist of Australian Trees'' lists four other common names: '''honeysuckle''', '''white banksia''', '''white bottlebrush''' and '''white honeysuckle''';<ref name=APNI>{{APNI|id=53918|title=''Banksia integrifolia''|access-date=19 November 2012}}</ref> and some older sources refer to it as '''honeysuckle oak'''.<ref name="Millett 1971">{{cite book | author = Millett, Mervyn | year = 1971 | title = Native Trees of Australia | location = Melbourne | publisher = Lansdowne | isbn = 0-7018-0394-0}}</ref><ref name="APCND">{{cite web | title = Australian plant common name database | publisher = [[Australian National Botanic Gardens]] | url = http://www.anbg.gov.au/common.names/index.html | access-date = 11 November 2006| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20061207012033/http://www.anbg.gov.au/common.names/index.html| archive-date = 7 December 2006 | url-status = live}}</ref>

It was known to [[Indigenous Australians]] before its discovery and naming by [[European exploration of Australia|Europeans]]; for example, the [[Gunai people|Gunai]] people of [[Gippsland]] called it '''{{lang|unn|birrna}}'''.<ref name="Museum Victoria">{{cite web | author = Museum Victoria | author-link = Museum Victoria | title = Aboriginal Plant Use | url = http://www.museum.vic.gov.au/infosheets/10319.pdf | access-date = 25 October 2006 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20060821090942/http://www.museum.vic.gov.au/infosheets/10319.pdf | archive-date = 21 August 2006 }}</ref> Because of its wide range it would have a name in a number of other [[Australian Aboriginal languages|indigenous languages]], but these are now lost. In 2001, a search of historical archives for recorded indigenous names of Victorian flora and fauna failed to find a single name for the species.<ref name="Wesson 2001">{{cite book | author = Wesson, Sue C. | year = 2001 | title = Aboriginal flora and fauna names of Victoria: As extracted from early surveyors' reports | location = Melbourne | publisher = Victorian Aboriginal Corporation for Languages | url = http://www.vaclang.org.au/admin/file/content9/c7/ff.pdf | access-date = 11 November 2006 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20060820093740/http://vaclang.org.au/admin/file/content9/c7/ff.pdf | archive-date = 20 August 2006}}</ref>

== Description ==
''B. integrifolia'' is a highly variable species. It is most often encountered as a tree up to {{convert|25|m|ft}} in height, but in sheltered locations it can reach {{convert|35|m|ft}}. In more exposed areas it may grow as a small, gnarled tree, reaching to no more than about {{convert|5|m|ft}}, and in highly exposed positions, such as on exposed coastal headlands, it may even be reduced to a small [[shrub]].<ref name="George 1999">{{cite encyclopedia | author = George, Alex S. | author-link = Alex George (botanist)  | year = 1999 | title = Banksia | editor = Wilson, Annette | encyclopedia = [[Flora of Australia (series)|Flora of Australia]] | volume = 17B: Proteaceae 3: Hakea to Dryandra | pages = 175–251 | publisher = CSIRO Publishing / [[Australian Biological Resources Study]] | isbn = 978-0-643-06454-6}}</ref>

The tree usually has a single stout [[trunk (botany)|trunk]], which is often twisted and gnarled, with the rough grey [[bark (botany)|bark]] characteristic of ''Banksia''. The leaves are dark green with a white underside, and occur in [[whorl (botany)|whorls]] of three to five. Adult leaves have entire margins. George specifies their dimensions as {{convert|4|–|20|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|6|–|35|mm|in|abbr=on}} wide,<ref name="George 1999"/><ref name="George 1981">{{The genus Banksia L.f. (Proteaceae)}}</ref> but ''[[The Banksia Atlas]]'' warns that "Atlas contributors found great variability in these measurements with specimens often falling outside the varietal limits specified by George (1981) or being intermediate between two varieties."<ref name ="Taylor 1988">{{The Banksia Atlas}}</ref> Juvenile leaves have dentate margins with a few short teeth, and are generally larger than adult leaves.<ref name="George 1999"/>

[[Flower]]s occur in ''Banksia'''s characteristic "flower spike", an [[inflorescence]] made up of several hundred flowers densely packed in a [[helix|spiral]] around a woody axis. This is roughly cylindrical, {{convert|10|–|12|cm|in|abbr=on}} high and {{convert|5|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide. Flowers are usually pale yellow to yellow, but may be greenish or pinkish in bud. Each individual flower consists of a tubular [[perianth]] made up of four united [[tepal]]s, and one long wiry [[carpel|style]]. Characteristic of the taxonomic section in which it is placed, the styles are straight rather than hooked. The style ends are initially trapped inside the upper perianth parts, but break free at [[anthesis]].<ref name="George 1999"/> This process starts with the flowers at the bottom of the inflorescence, sweeping up the spike at an unusually high rate of between 96 and 390 flowers per 24 hours.<ref name="McFarland 1985">{{cite journal | author = McFarland, David C. | year = 1985 | title = Flowering Biology and Phenology of Banksia integrifolia and B. spinulosa (Proteaceae) in New England National Park, N.S.W | journal = [[Australian Journal of Botany]] | volume = 33 | pages = 705–714 | doi = 10.1071/BT9850705 | issue = 6 | bibcode = 1985AuJB...33..705M }}</ref>

The flower spikes are not as prominent as in some other ''Banksia'' species, as they arise from two- to three-year-old nodes nested within the foliage. After flowering, old flower parts wither and fall away over a period of several months, revealing the "cone", a woody axis embedded with many small [[follicle (fruit)|follicles]]. The follicles are initially greenish and downy, but gradually fade to dark grey. Each follicle contains one or sometimes two [[seed]]s, separated by a thin wooden [[Seed separator|separator]]. The seed itself is black, {{convert|6|–|10|mm|in|abbr=on}} long with a feathery black 'wing' {{convert|10|–|20|mm|in|abbr=on|1}} long.<ref name="George 1999"/><ref name="George 1981"/>

''B. integrifolia'' was first collected at [[Botany Bay]] on 29 April 1770, by [[Joseph Banks|Sir Joseph Banks]] and [[Daniel Solander|Dr Daniel Solander]], naturalists on the ''[[HMS Endeavour|Endeavour]]'' during Lieutenant (later Captain) [[James Cook]]'s [[First voyage of James Cook|first voyage]] to the Pacific Ocean.<ref name="Wharton 1893">{{cite book | editor = William J. L. Wharton | year = 1893 | title = [[Wikisource:Captain Cook's Journal, First Voyage|Captain Cook's Journal during his First Voyage Round the World made in H. M. Bark "Endeavour" 1768–71: A Literal Transcription of the Original MSS]] | location = London | publisher = E. Stock}}</ref><ref name="Banks 1770">{{cite web | author = Banks, Joseph | author-link = Joseph Banks | title = 29 April 1770 | work = Banks's Journal | url = http://southseas.nla.gov.au/journals/banks/17700429.html | access-date = 25 October 2006| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20061008005340/http://southseas.nla.gov.au/journals/banks/17700429.html| archive-date= 8 October 2006 | url-status= live}}</ref> Solander coined the (unpublished) binomial name ''Leucadendrum integrifolium'' in ''[[Banks' Florilegium]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Diment |first1=Judith A. |author-link1=Judith Diment |last2=Humphries |first2=Christopher J. |author-link2=Chris Humphries |last3=Newington |first3=Linda |last4=Shaughnessy |first4=Elaine |journal=[[Bulletin of the British Museum (Natural History)]] |series=Historical Series |title=Catalogue of the Natural History drawings commissioned by Joseph Banks on the Endeavour Voyage 1768–1771 held in the British Museum (Natural History): Part 1: Botany: Australia |volume=11 (Complete) |pages=1–183 [149]|publisher=[[British Museum (Natural History)]] |publication-place=London |date=1984 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/2355050 |doi=10.5962/p.310430|doi-access=free }}</ref> However, the species was not published until April 1782, when [[Carolus Linnaeus the Younger]] described the first four ''Banksia'' species in his ''[[Supplementum Plantarum]]''. Linnaeus distinguished the species by their leaf shapes, and named them accordingly. Thus the species with [[Leaf#Margins (edge)|entire leaf margins]] was given the specific name ''integrifolia'', from the [[Latin]] {{lang|la|integer}} meaning 'entire' and {{lang|la|folium}} 'leaf'.<ref name="L.f. 1782">{{cite book | author = Carolus Linnaeus the Younger | author-link = Carolus Linnaeus the Younger | year = 1782 | title = Supplementum Plantarum | location = Brunsvigae | publisher = Orphanotrophei|url=http://botanicus.org/page/411160 | page=127}}</ref> The [[Binomial nomenclature#Authority|full name]] for the species is therefore ''Banksia integrifolia'' L.f.<ref name="APNI"/>

Then followed around 200 years of confusion over the taxonomic limits of the species, caused by the species' great variability, similarities with closely related species, and early attempts to classify the species based on dried specimen material alone. A stable ''Banksia'' taxonomy did not begin to emerge until 1981 with the publication of [[Alex George (botanist)|Alex George]]'s landmark monograph ''[[The genus Banksia L.f. (Proteaceae)]]''. Over the next 18 years, George's arrangement was gradually refined in the light of new research and the discovery of new material, and there were several changes to ''B. integrifolia''{{'}}s infraspecific taxa.<ref name="George 1986">{{cite journal | author = George, Alex S. | author-link = Alex George (botanist) | year = 1996 | title = Notes on ''Banksia'' L. f | journal = [[Nuytsia (journal)|Nuytsia]] | volume = 11 | issue = 1 | pages = 21–24| doi = 10.58828/nuy00249 | s2cid = 181990314 | url = https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/part/236375 }}</ref><ref name="Thiele 1996">{{cite journal | last1 = Thiele | first1 = Kevin | author-link1 = Kevin Thiele | last2 = Ladiges | first2 = Pauline Y. | author-link2 = Pauline Ladiges | year = 1996 | title = A Cladistic Analysis of Banksia (Proteaceae) | journal = [[Australian Systematic Botany]] | volume = 9 | issue = 5 | pages = 661–733 | doi = 10.1071/SB9960661 | bibcode = 1996AuSyB...9..661T }}</ref> These changes culminated in George's 1999 arrangement, which had broad acceptance until 2005, when [[Austin Mast]], Eric Jones and Shawn Havery published a [[phylogeny]] that did not accord with George's arrangement.<ref name="Mast 2005">{{cite journal | last1 = Mast | first1 = Austin R. | author-link1=Austin Mast | first2=Eric H. |last2=Jones |first3=Shawn P. | last3=Havery | year = 2005 | volume = 18 | issue = 1 | title = An Assessment of Old and New DNA sequence evidence for the Paraphyly of Banksia with respect to Dryandra (Proteaceae) | journal = [[Australian Systematic Botany]] | pages = 75–88 | publisher = CSIRO Publishing / Australian Systematic Botany Society | doi = 10.1071/SB04015 | bibcode = 2005AuSyB..18...75M }}</ref> A new taxonomic arrangement was not published at the time, but early in 2007 Mast and Thiele initiated a rearrangement by transferring ''[[Dryandra]]'' to ''Banksia'', and publishing [[Banksia subg. Spathulatae|''B.'' subg. ''Spathulatae'']] for the species having spoon-shaped [[cotyledon]]s. They foreshadowed publishing a full arrangement once DNA [[sampling (statistics)|sampling]] of ''Dryandra'' was complete. In the meantime, if Mast and Thiele's nomenclatural changes are taken as an interim arrangement, then ''B. integrifolia'' is placed in ''B.'' subg. ''Spathulatae''; it is the type species for the subgenus.<ref name="Mast 2007">{{cite journal | last1=Mast | first1=Austin R. | last2=Thiele | first2=Kevin | year = 2007 | title = The transfer of Dryandra R.Br. to Banksia L.f. (Proteaceae) | journal = [[Australian Systematic Botany]] | volume = 20 | issue=1 | pages = 63–71 | doi = 10.1071/SB06016 | bibcode=2007AuSyB..20...63M }}</ref>

=== Placement within ''Banksia'' ===
The current taxonomic arrangement of the genus ''Banksia'' is based on George's 1999 monograph for the ''[[Flora of Australia (series)|Flora of Australia]]'' book series.<ref name="George 1999"/> In this arrangement, ''B. integrifolia'' is placed in [[Banksia subg. Banksia|''Banksia'' subg. ''Banksia'']], because its inflorescences take the form of ''Banksia''{{'}}s characteristic flower spikes; [[Banksia sect. Banksia|''Banksia'' sect. ''Banksia'']] because of its straight [[carpel|styles]]; and [[Banksia ser. Salicinae|''Banksia'' ser. ''Salicinae'']] because its inflorescences are cylindrical. Kevin Thiele additionally placed it in a subseries ''Integrifoliae'',<ref name="Thiele 1996"/> but this was not supported by George.

=== Subspecies ===

* [[Banksia integrifolia subsp. compar|''B. integrifolia'' subsp. ''compar'']] <small>([[R.Br.]]) [[K.R.Thiele]]</small>;<ref name=APC1>{{cite web|title=''Banksia integrifolia'' subsp. ''compar''|url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/140128|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=8 May 2020}}</ref>
* [[Banksia integrifolia subsp. integrifolia|''B. integrifolia'' <small>R.Br.</small>subsp. ''integrifolia'']];<ref name=APC2>{{cite web|title=''Banksia integrifolia'' subsp. ''integrifolia''|url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/140519|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=8 May 2020}}</ref>
* [[Banksia integrifolia subsp. monticola|''B. integrifolia'' subsp. ''monticola'']] <small>K.R.Thiele</small>.<ref name=APC3>{{cite web|title=''Banksia integrifolia'' subsp. ''monticola''|url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/141261|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=8 May 2020}}</ref>

Although some of the great variability of ''B. integrifolia'' can be attributed to environmental factors, much is [[genetics|genetic]]: George writes that it "gives the impression that it is actively speciating to fill the many ecological niches through its range".<ref name="George 1981"/> Genetic variation across its range has been mapped in some detail with [[microsatellite]] markers, facilitating further analysis of intraspecific relationships.<ref>{{cite journal |ref=no |last1=Fatemi |first1=Mohammad |last2=Houliston |first2=Gary J. |last3=Haddadchi |first3=Azadeh |last4=Gross |first4=Caroline L. |title=Cost-effective microsatellite markers for Banksia integrifolia (Proteaceae) |journal=Applications in Plant Sciences |year=2013 |volume=1 |issue=2 |article-number=1200130 |doi=10.3732/apps.1200130 |pmid=25202510 |pmc=4105364 |bibcode=2013AppPS...100130F |doi-access=free }}</ref> [[Fractal analysis]] of the shape and spectrum (colour) of the leaves has been used to determine to which subspecies plants of unknown provenance belong.<ref>{{cite journal |ref=no |last1=Pandolfi |first1=Camilla |last2=Messina |first2=Giuseppe |last3=Mugnai |first3=Sergio |last4=Azzarello |first4=Elisa |last5=Masi |first5=Elisa |last6=Dixon |first6=Kingsley |last7=Mancuso |first7=Stefano |title=Discrimination and identification of morphotypes of Banksia integrifolia (Proteaceae) by an Artificial Neural Network (ANN), based on morphological and fractal parameters of leaves and flowers |journal=Taxon |volume=58 |issue=3 |pages=925–933 |year=2009 |doi=10.1002/tax.583020 |bibcode=2009Taxon..58..925P |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/tax.583020|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

;''Banksia integrifolia'' subsp. ''integrifolia''
:The nominate subspecies occurs near the coast over most of the species' range except the far north. It varies little except in northern [[New South Wales]] and southern [[Queensland]], where some populations appear to be intermediate with ''B. integrifolia'' subsp. ''compar''.
;''Banksia integrifolia'' subsp. ''compar''
:This subspecies grows in coastal Queensland as far north as [[Proserpine, Queensland|Proserpine]]. For most of its range it is the only subspecies, but near its southern limit it co-occurs with ''B. integrifolia'' subsp. ''integrifolia''. The two subspecies are distinguishable by their leaves, which are larger and glossy with wavy margins on ''B. integrifolia'' subsp. ''compar''.
;''Banksia integrifolia'' subsp. ''monticola''
:Commonly known as white mountain banksia, it is the only subspecies with a [[montane]] distribution; it occurs in the [[Blue Mountains (Australia)|Blue Mountains]] of New South Wales. It is similar in form to ''B. integrifolia'' subsp. ''integrifolia'', but differs in having longer, narrower leaves, and follicles that are more deeply embedded in the old flower spike.<ref name ="Harden 2000">{{cite book | author = Harden G. J. | author2 = D. W. Hardin | author3 = D. C. Godden | name-list-style = amp | year = 2000 | title = Proteaceae of New South Wales | publisher = UNSW Press | isbn = 978-0-86840-302-1}}</ref>

=== Hybrids ===
Presumed natural [[hybrid (biology)|hybrids]] have been reported between ''B. integrifolia'' and other members of [[Banksia ser. Salicinae|''Banksia'' ser. ''Salicinae'']], although no [[hybrid name (botany)|hybrid names]] have been formally published to date. Presumed hybrids are identified by their intermediate features; for example those with ''[[Banksia paludosa|B. paludosa]]'' (swamp banksia), known from [[Jervis Bay Territory|Jervis Bay]] and [[Green Cape, New South Wales|Green Cape]] on the coast of southern New South Wales, have a smaller habit, longer, thinner flower spikes, and persistent old flowers on old "cones", which are otherwise bare on pure ''B. integrifolia''.<ref name="Liber 2005">{{cite journal |author=Liber, C. |year=2005 |title=''Banksia paludosa paludosa'' in the Jervis Bay Area |journal=Banksia Study Group Newsletter |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=4–5 |url=http://asgap.org.au/banksSG/banksiasg-6-2.pdf |access-date=31 October 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070904223149/http://asgap.org.au/banksSG/banksiasg-6-2.pdf |archive-date=4 September 2007 }}</ref><ref name="Salkin 1979">
Salkin, Abraham Isaac (Alf) (1979). "Variation in ''Banksia'' in Eastern Australia". (MSc thesis). Clayton, Victoria: Monash University.</ref><ref name="Liber 2004b">{{cite journal|author=Liber, C. |year=2004 |title=''Banksia integrifolia'' x ''paludosa'' hybrids at Green Cape |journal=Banksia Study Group Newsletter |volume=6 |pages=8–9 |url=http://asgap.org.au/banksSG/banksiasg-6-1.pdf |access-date=31 October 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070904223329/http://asgap.org.au/banksSG/banksiasg-6-1.pdf |archive-date=4 September 2007}}</ref>

Presumed hybrids with ''[[Banksia marginata|B. marginata]]'' (silver banksia) occur on [[Wilsons Promontory]] in Victoria; these are found in localities where both species co-occur, and have features intermediate between the two.<ref name="George 1981"/> Another purported hybrid with ''B. marginata'', thought to be from [[Cape Paterson, Victoria|Cape Paterson]] on Victoria's south coast, was first described by Alf Salkin and is commercially available in small quantities. It forms an attractive hardy low-growing plant to {{convert|1|m|ft}}.<ref name="Salkin 1986">{{cite journal | author = Salkin, Alf | year = 1986 | title = Banksia Cultivars | journal = Banksia Study Report | issue = 7 | pages = 17–19 | publisher = [[ASGAP]] | issn = 0728-2893}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
''B. integrifolia'' is widely distributed, in both [[geography of Australia|geographical]] and [[ecology|ecological]] terms. According to Alex George, "it spans a wider geographical and [[Climate of Australia|climatic]] range than any other species."<ref name="George 1981"/> Thiele and [[Pauline Ladiges|Ladiges]] make a similar claim: that its distribution "is a broader latitudinal, altitudinal and ecological amplitude than any other species, with the possible exception of ''[[Banksia spinulosa|B. spinulosa]]''."<ref name="Thiele 1994">{{cite journal | last1=Thiele | first1=Kevin | first2=Pauline |last2=Ladiges | year = 1994 | title = The Banksia integrifolia L.f. Species Complex (Proteaceae) | journal = [[Australian Systematic Botany]] | volume = 7 | pages = 393–408 | doi = 10.1071/SB9940393 | issue = 4 | bibcode=1994AuSyB...7..393T }}</ref> No other species of tree occurs closer to the coast at [[Cape Byron]], making ''B. integrifolia'' the most easterly tree on the Australian mainland.<ref name ="Mason 1999">{{cite book | author = Mason, D. | year = 1999 | title = The Blooming Banksia: Easy Identification of Banksias in Far North Eastern NSW and South Eastern Qld.| publisher = [[Australian Plants Society]], NSW Region – Far North Coast Group | location = [[Lismore, New South Wales|Lismore]] | isbn = 978-0-909830-51-9}}</ref>

[[File:Banksia integrifolia integrifolia Manly2 email.jpg|thumb|right|Tree on headland, [[Manly, New South Wales|Manly]], NSW]]

It occurs along almost the entire eastern coast of Australia, from [[Geelong, Victoria]] to [[Proserpine, Queensland]]. There was an isolated population on [[Long Island (Tasmania)|Long Island]], [[Tasmania]] in 1999, and an 1876 record allegedly from [[King Island (Tasmania)|King Island]],<ref name="George 1999"/> although there has been speculation that that specimen was actually collected in the [[Furneaux Group]].<ref name="Barnes 2004">{{cite journal |author=Barnes, Richard |year=2004 |title=Evidence for ''Banksia integrifolia'' in Tasmania |journal=Banksia Study Group Newsletter |volume=6 |page=8 |url=http://asgap.org.au/banksSG/banksiasg-6-1.pdf |access-date=1 November 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070904223329/http://asgap.org.au/banksSG/banksiasg-6-1.pdf |archive-date=4 September 2007}}</ref> The species no longer occurs at any of these Tasmania locations, and has been declared [[List of extinct flora of Australia#Tasmania|extinct in Tasmania]] under that state's ''[[Threatened Species Protection Act 1995]]''.<ref name="DPIW">{{cite web | title = Threatened Species List – Vascular Plants A-B | publisher = [[Department of Primary Industries and Water]], Tasmanian Government | url = http://www.dpiw.tas.gov.au/inter.nsf/WebPages/SLEN-5P27QC?open | access-date = 28 March 2007}}</ref> The range of latitude is thus about [[20th parallel south|20°]] to [[38th parallel south|38°S]].

For most of its distribution, ''B. integrifolia'' occurs only within about {{cvt|50|km|mi}} of the coast, where it typically occurs on poor quality sandy soils derived from [[sandstone]]. It grows near coastal cliffs and headlands, alongside river [[estuary|estuaries]], and even on stabilised sand dunes. The temperature range for this area is around {{cvt|0–30|C|F}}, with almost no [[frost]]s. The species can occur in pure stands, but is usually associated with other species such as ''[[Melaleuca quinquenervia]]'' (broad-leaved paperbark),<ref name ="Taylor 1988" /><ref name="Boland 1992">{{cite book | author = Boland, D. J. | year = 1992 | title = Forest Trees of Australia (Fourth edition revised and enlarged) | publisher = CSIRO Publishing | location = Collingwood, Victoria | isbn = 978-0-643-05423-3 | display-authors = etal}}</ref> ''[[Angophora costata]]'' (smooth-barked apple), ''[[Corymbia gummifera]]'' (red bloodwood), ''[[Eucalyptus botryoides]]'' (bangalay), ''[[Monotoca elliptica]]'' (wedding bush) and ''[[Leptospermum laevigatum]]'' (coast tea tree).<ref name=Benson2000>{{cite journal|last1=Benson|first1=Doug|last2=McDougall|first2=Lyn|year=2000|title=Ecology of Sydney Plant Species Part 7b: Dicotyledon families Proteaceae to Rubiaceae|journal=Cunninghamia|volume=6|issue=4|pages=1017–1202 [1032–1033]|url=https://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/getmedia/eea3e2c5-4590-49ce-9114-4b7e8527d491/Volume-6(4)-2000-Cun6Ben1016-1202.pdf.aspx|access-date=19 January 2021|archive-date=28 December 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211228100224/https://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/getmedia/eea3e2c5-4590-49ce-9114-4b7e8527d491/Volume-6(4)-2000-Cun6Ben1016-1202.pdf.aspx}}</ref>

Between [[Sydney]] and [[Brisbane]], ''B. integrifolia'' is found up to {{cvt|200|km|mi}} inland, with ''B. integrifolia'' subsp. ''monticola'' occurring in the Blue Mountains at altitudes up to {{cvt|1,500|m|ft}}. There it grows on better quality volcanic or rocky soils derived from [[granite]]s and [[basalt]]s, and would experience up to 100 frosts per year. In this montane habitat, it occurs in association with ''[[Eucalyptus]]'' species such as [[Eucalyptus viminalis|''E. viminalis'']] (manna gum) and [[Eucalyptus pauciflora|''E. pauciflora'']] (snow gum), and also [[rainforest]] species such as ''[[Nothofagus moorei]]'' (Antarctic beech) and ''[[Orites excelsa]]'' (prickly ash).<ref name="Taylor 1988"/><ref name="Boland 1992"/>

== Ecology ==
{{see also|Ecology of Banksia}}
[[File:Littlewattlebird2.jpg|right|thumb|''Anthochaera chrysoptera'' ([[little wattlebird]]) on ''B. integrifolia'']]
[[File:20050219 Chelsea LorikeetInBanksia.jpg|right|thumb|''Trichoglossus moluccanus'' ([[rainbow lorikeet]]) on ''B. integrifolia'']]
Like most other [[Proteaceae]], ''B. integrifolia'' has [[proteoid root]]s, i.e., roots with dense clusters of short lateral rootlets that form a mat in the soil just below the leaf litter. These enhance [[solubility|solubilisation]] of nutrients, thus allowing nutrient uptake in low-nutrient soils such as the [[phosphorus]]-deficient native soils of Australia. Studies on ''B. integrifolia'' suggest that its proteoid root mat achieves this by chemically modifying its soil environment.<ref name="Grierson 1989">{{cite journal | author = "Grierson, P.F. | author2 = P. M. Attiwill |name-list-style = amp | year = 1989 | title = Chemical characteristics of the proteoid root mat of Banksia integrifolia L. {{sic}} | journal = [[Australian Journal of Botany]] | volume = 37 | pages = 137–143 | doi = 10.1071/BT9890137 | issue = 2 | bibcode = 1989AuJB...37..137G }}</ref>

''B. integrifolia'' flowers have an unusually short life span for ''Banksia'' species, producing [[nectar]] for only about four to twelve days after anthesis. Most nectar is produced during the night and early in the morning, with only small amounts produced during the day.<ref name="McFarland 1985"/> Flowers are produced all through the year, but there is a strong peak in autumn. Little else flowers within its range at this time, so it is a seasonally important source of food for [[nectarivore|nectariferous]] animals. Surveys have observed a range of animals feeding on the species, including a wide range of [[insect]]s; many species of bird including ''[[Phylidonyris novaehollandiae]]'' (New Holland honeyeater), ''[[Anthochaera carunculata]]'' (red wattlebird), ''[[Anthochaera chrysoptera]]'' (little wattlebird), ''[[Acanthorhynchus tenuirostris]]'' (eastern spinebill) and ''[[Trichoglossus moluccanus]]'' (rainbow lorikeet); and mammals such as ''[[Petaurus norfolcensis]]'' (squirrel glider), ''[[Petaurus breviceps]]'' (sugar glider), ''[[Acrobates pygmaeus]]'' (feathertail glider), ''[[Pteropus poliocephalus]]'' (grey-headed flying fox),<ref name="Taylor 1988"/><ref name="Hackett 2001">{{cite journal |author1=Hackett, Damian J. |author2=Goldingay, Ross L. | year = 2001 | title = Pollination of ''Banksia'' spp. by non-flying mammals in North-eastern New South Wales | journal = [[Australian Journal of Botany]] | volume = 49 | pages = 637–644 | doi = 10.1071/BT00004 | issue = 5 |bibcode=2001AuJB...49..637H }}</ref> and ''Syconycteris australis'' ([[common blossom bat]]).<ref>{{cite journal |ref=no |last1=Drury |first1=Rebecca L. |last2=Geister |first2=Fritz |title=Activity patterns and roosting of the eastern blossom-bat (Syconycteris australis) |journal=Australian Mammalogy |year=2014 |volume=36 |issue=1 |pages=29–34 |doi=10.1071/AM13025 |url=https://www.publish.csiro.au/am/am13025|doi-access=free }}</ref> In some areas such as at [[Bungawalbin National Park]] in northern New South Wales, ''B. integrifolia'' is the only source of nectar and pollen in the autumn (March–April) and late winter (July).<ref>{{cite journal | title=Feeding behaviour of the squirrel glider at Bungawalbin Nature Reserve, north-eastern New South Wales | author1=Sharpe, D.J. | author2=Goldingay, Ross L. | journal=Wildlife Research | volume=25 | issue=3 | pages=243–54 | doi=10.1071/WR97037 | year=1998 | bibcode=1998WildR..25..243S }}</ref> The importance of non-flying mammals to pollination of ''B. integrifolia'' was demonstrated in 1989, with a study in [[Wilsons Promontory National Park]] showing a reduction of fruit set when measures were taken to exclude them.<ref name="Cunningham 1991">{{cite journal | author = Cunningham, S. A. | year = 1991 | title = Experimental evidence for pollination of ''Banksia'' spp. by non-flying mammals | journal = [[Oecologia]] | volume = 87 | issue = 1 | pages = 86–90 | doi = 10.1007/BF00323784 | pmid = 28313356 | bibcode = 1991Oecol..87...86C | s2cid = 35237880 }}</ref> ''Banksia integrifolia'' is the host plant of the [[lichen]] species ''[[Arthonia banksiae]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |ref=no |last1=Kantvilas |first1=Gintaras |last2=Stajsic |first2=Val |title=Arthonia banksiae (lichenised Ascomycota) and its synonyms |journal=Muelleria |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=27–32 |year=2011 |doi=10.5962/p.292509 |s2cid=54914271 |url=https://www.rbg.vic.gov.au/documents/Muelleria_29(1),_Kantvilas__Stajsic.pdf |access-date=3 April 2021 |archive-date=9 April 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200409194642/https://www.rbg.vic.gov.au/documents/Muelleria_29%281%29%2C_Kantvilas__Stajsic.pdf }}</ref> 
Microscopic Eriophyid mites ([[Eriophyidae]]) cause [[gall]]s on young [[infructescence]]s of ''B. integrifolia.''<ref>Jones, David L. Elliot, W. Rodger, Jones, Sandra R., & Blake, Trevor L. (2015). "Pests, diseases, ailments and allies of Australian plants : an introduction to some of the good, bad and interesting creatures that you might find in your garden; with aids to their identification, symptoms and recommendations for control". Reed New Holland Publishers Pty Ltd. p. 173.</ref>
[[File:Galls Banksia integrifolia2021.jpg|thumb|Galls caused by an Eriophyid mite ([[Eriophyidae]]) on ''Banksia integrifolia'' [[infructescence]] in [[Melbourne]], Australia]]

Unlike most ''Banksia'' species, ''B. integrifolia'' does not require [[Bushfires in Australia|bushfire]] to trigger the release of its seed. Rather, seed is released spontaneously on reaching maturity in late summer. The species' non-reliance on fire for seed dispersal suggests that the exclusion of fire would not affect plant populations, but a number of studies have found the opposite to be true: in areas where fire has been excluded for many years, populations have declined substantially. An investigation into the defoliation and premature death of trees on the [[Yanakie Isthmus]] in south Victoria reached the tentative conclusion that the absence of fire had created unhealthy surface soil conditions.<ref name="Bennett 1996">{{cite journal | last1 = Bennett | first1 = L. T. | first2 = P. M. | last2 = Attiwill | year = 1996 | title = The Nutritional Status of Healthy and Declining Stands of ''Banksia Integrifolia'' on the Yanakie Isthmus, Victoria | journal = [[Australian Journal of Botany]] | volume = 45 | pages = 15–30 | doi = 10.1071/BT96025}}</ref> On the [[Mornington Peninsula]], surveys of an area that had not been burnt since the 1890s found that ''B. integrifolia'' densities fell by 77% between 1977 and 2000. A subsequent study found the decline to have been caused by extremely high seedling mortality rates, due to grazing by [[herbivore]]s and intense competition for soil moisture during summer. Despite acknowledging that "the role of fire in these systems remains unclear", it concluded that "developing fire and/or grazing management regimes will be necessary to conserve the structural integrity of these coastal ecosystems."<ref name="Price 2003">{{cite journal | author1 = Price, J. N. | author2 = J. W. Morgan | name-list-style = amp | year = 2003 | title = Mechanisms controlling establishment of the non-bradysporous Banksia integrifolia (Coast Banksia) in an unburnt coastal woodland | journal = [[Austral Ecology]] | volume = 28 | issue = 1 | pages = 82–92 | doi = 10.1046/j.1442-9993.2003.01252.x | bibcode = 2003AusEc..28...82P }}</ref>

These concerns aside, ''B. integrifolia'' does not appear to be under threat. It is highly resistant to ''[[Phytophthora cinnamomi]]'' dieback, which poses a major threat to many other ''Banksia'' species;<ref name="McCredie 1985">{{cite journal | last1 = McCredie | first1 = T. A. | first2 = K. W. | last2 = Dixon | first3 = K. | last3 = Sivasithamparam | year = 1985 | title = Variability in the resistance of Banksia L.f. species to Phytophthora cinnamomi Rands | journal = [[Australian Journal of Botany]] | volume = 33 | pages = 629–637 | doi = 10.1071/BT9850629 | issue = 6 | bibcode = 1985AuJB...33..629M }}</ref> and its wide distribution protects against the threat of habitat loss due to land clearing. As a result, it does not appear on the [[list of threatened flora of Australia]] under the [[Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999]].

== Cultivation ==
[[File:B integrifolia roller coaster sylvan1 email.jpg|thumb|right|upright=.8|''B.'' 'Roller Coaster', Sylvan Grove Gardens, [[Picnic Point, New South Wales]]]]
Hardy and versatile, ''B. integrifolia'' will grow in [[clay]], [[sand]], [[acid]] and even [[alkali]]ne soils, and it shows good resistance to wind and [[salt]], making it suitable for seaside planting.<ref name="Elliot 1982">{{cite book | last1 = Elliot | first1 = R. | last2 = Jones | first2 = D. L. | year = 1982 | title = Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation | publisher = Lothian Press | location = Melbourne | isbn = 978-0-85091-143-5}}</ref> It is therefore highly regarded as a low-maintenance garden tree, although its large size makes it unsuitable for smaller gardens. Its hardiness may, however, forewarn weed potential, as some evidence of weediness has been seen in South Africa,<ref>{{cite journal |ref=no |last1=Moodley |first1=Desika |last2=Geerts |first2=Sjirk |last3=Rebelo |first3=Tony |last4=Richardson |first4=David M. |last5=Wilson |first5=John R. U. |title=Site-specific conditions influence plant naturalization: The case of alien Proteaceae in South Africa |journal=Acta Oecologica |volume=59 |year=2014 |pages=62–71 |doi=10.1016/j.actao.2014.05.005 |bibcode=2014AcO....59...62M |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1146609X14000630|hdl=10019.1/112274 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> [[Western Australia]] and New Zealand.<ref>{{cite journal |ref=no |last1=Keighery |first1=Greg |last2=Keighery |first2=Bronwen |title=Banksia behaving badly |journal=Western Australian Naturalist |year=2015 |pages=270–277 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/283353093}}</ref> When growing near bushland within its native habitat, it is suggested to obtain local provenance plants if available.<ref name="Liber 2002">{{cite magazine | last = Liber | first = Cas | year = 2002 | title = Banksias as weeds |magazine= Banksia Study Group Newsletter | volume = 4 | issue = 1 | pages = 4–5 |publisher=Association of Societies for Growing Australian Plants |issn=1444-285X |url=https://anpsa.org.au/newsletter/banksia-study-group/ |format=PDF}}</ref>

The most common form available in commercial nurseries is unimproved ''Banksia integrifolia'' subsp. ''integrifolia''. It prefers a sunny aspect without exposure to frosts, and tolerates fairly heavy [[pruning]]. Seeds do not require any treatment, and take 5 to 6 weeks to [[germinate]].<ref name="Sweedman 2006">{{cite book | last = Sweedman | first = Luke | year = 2006 | title = Australian seeds: a guide to their collection, identification and biology | url = https://archive.org/details/australianseedsg00auth | url-access = limited | publisher = CSIRO Publishing | isbn = 0-643-09298-6 | page = [https://archive.org/details/australianseedsg00auth/page/n219 203]|display-authors=etal}}</ref> Flowering begins at around four to six years from seed. The other subspecies are less well known in cultivation, but are obtainable. Cultivation is presumably similar to ''B. integrifolia'' subsp. ''integrifolia'',<ref name="George 1987">{{The Banksia Book}}</ref> except that ''B. integrifolia'' subsp. ''monticola'' may be assumed frost-tolerant. [[Dwarfing|Dwarf]] forms of ''B. integrifolia'' are sometimes sold, and a registered prostrate [[cultivar]], [[Banksia 'Roller Coaster'|''Banksia'' 'Roller Coaster']], is available. The latter is a vigorous ground-hugging plant that can spread to {{convert|4 or 5|m}} across yet remains only {{convert|50|cm|abbr=on}} high.<ref name="ACRA">{{cite web |author=Australian Cultivar Registration Authority |author-link=Australian Cultivar Registration Authority |title=Banksia 'Roller Coaster' |work=Descriptions of registered cultivars |url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc404.html |access-date=7 November 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060906011003/http://anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc404.html |archive-date=6 September 2006}}</ref>

Because of its high resistance to ''P. cinnamomi'' dieback, the feasibility of using ''B. integrifolia'' as a rootstock for susceptible ''Banksia'' species in the [[floriculture|cut flower trade]] is under investigation. Presently, the success rate for grafting is only 30–40%, and even with successful grafts there is a tendency for the union to fail under stress. More research is needed before the technique will be ready for commercial use.<ref name="Sedgley 1996">{{cite book | author = Sedgley, Margaret | year = 1996 | chapter = Banksia, Family Proteaceae | pages = 18–35 | editor1 = Krystyna A. Johnson | editor2 = Margaret Burchett | title = Native Australian Plants: Horticulture and Uses | location = Sydney | publisher = University of New South Wales Press | isbn = 978-0-86840-159-1}}</ref>

== Other uses ==
[[File:B integrifolia compar.jpg|thumb|right|''B. integrifolia'' subsp. ''compar'']]

The [[wood]] of ''B. integrifolia'' is pink to red, with inconspicuous [[growth ring|rings]] and conspicuous rays. It is spongy and porous, with a density of around {{convert|530|kg/m3|lb/ft3|abbr=on}}. It is considered highly decorative, but it warps badly on drying,<ref name="Boland 1992"/> has poor load-bearing qualities, and is susceptible to [[termite]] attack;<ref name="George 1987"/> it is therefore unsuitable for most construction purposes. It is sometimes used for cabinet panelling and in ornamental [[woodturning|turnery]], and natural bends were once sought after for making boat [[knee (construction)|knees]].<ref name="Cribb 1981">{{cite book | author = Cribb, A.B. | author2 = Cribb, J.W. | year = 1981 | title = Useful Wild Plants in Australia | location = Sydney | publisher = Collins | isbn = 978-0-00-216441-2}}</ref> It is a useful [[wood fuel|firewood]].<ref name="Species Bank">{{cite web | title = Banksia integrifolia (Family Proteaceae) | work = Speciesbank | publisher = [[Department of the Environment and Heritage]] | url = http://www.environment.gov.au/cgi-bin/species-bank/sbank-treatment2.pl?id=12557 | access-date = 27 February 2007}}</ref>

''B. integrifolia'' produces a dark amber-coloured [[honey]] of middling quality and therefore low commercial value.<ref name="Boland 1992"/> Despite this, the species is highly valued by [[beekeeping|beekeepers]] because it produces large amounts of pollen and nectar during autumn and winter, thus helping support [[beehive (beekeeping)|hives]] at a time when little else is flowering.<ref name="Cribb 1981"/>

Historically, [[indigenous Australians]] obtained nectar from ''B. integrifolia'' by stroking the flower spikes then licking their hands, or by steeping flower spikes in a [[coolamon (vessel)|coolamon]] overnight. They also used the flower spikes as [[hairbrush]]es. Early settlers used the nectar as a syrup for sore throats and colds;<ref name="RBGES">{{cite web | title = Aboriginal Resources Trail Teachers' Kit | publisher = Royal Botanical Gardens Melbourne, Education Section | url = http://www.rbg.vic.gov.au/__data/page/1062/ART.pdf | access-date = 10 November 2006|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20061002082815/http://www.rbg.vic.gov.au/__data/page/1062/ART.pdf | archive-date = 2 October 2006 }}</ref> and bushmen would impregnate barren "cones" with fat to make a slow-burning [[candle]].<ref name="Cribb 1981"/>

More recently, ''B. integrifolia'' has been used in the art of [[bonsai]]. Its rangy habit and long internodes are challenging to overcome, but the leaves do reduce with pruning, and unlike the gnarlier ''[[Banksia serrata|B. serrata]]'' (saw banksia) its trunk can become textured with age.<ref name="Bowie 2002">{{cite journal | last = Bowie | first = G. | year = 2002 | title = The Banksia as Bonsai: ''B. integrifolia'' | journal = ASGAP Australian Plants as Bonsai Study Group Newsletter | issue = 3 | pages = 4–6 | url = http://asgap.org.au/APOL31/sep03-5.html | access-date = 25 October 2006 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070905222805/http://asgap.org.au/APOL31/sep03-5.html | archive-date = 5 September 2007}}</ref><ref name="ANPAB">{{cite web | publisher = [[Australian National Botanic Gardens]] | title = Australian Native Plants as Bonsai | url = http://www.anbg.gov.au/bonsai/ | access-date = 14 November 2006}}</ref>

It is used as a [[floral emblem]] by two [[local government areas of Queensland]]: the [[Redcliffe, Queensland|City of Redcliffe]]<ref name="Discover Redcliffe">{{cite web | title = Discover Redcliffe | url = http://www.redcliffe.qld.gov.au/_Brochure_reprint_RCC.pdf | access-date = 25 October 2006 | publisher = Redcliffe City Council | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20060825105142/http://www.redcliffe.qld.gov.au/_Brochure_reprint_RCC.pdf | archive-date = 25 August 2006}}</ref> and the [[Logan City, Queensland|City of Logan]].<ref name="Buchanan 1999">{{cite web | author = Buchanan, Robyn | year = 1999 | title = City insignia | work = Logan: Rich in History, Young in Spirit | publisher = Logan City Council | url = http://www.logan.qld.gov.au/NR/rdonlyres/D708EF30-53B4-49C0-808E-0C7DE6748D95/0/RichinHistoryCityinsignia.pdf | access-date = 25 October 2006|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20061012163233/http://www.logan.qld.gov.au/LCC/logan/history/historycomprehensive.htm | archive-date = 12 October 2006 }}</ref> In 2000 it was featured on an [[Postage stamps and postal history of Australia|Australian postage stamp]].<ref name="ANBG stamps">{{cite web | title = Banksia integrifolia var. integrifolia | work = Flora on stamps | publisher = [[Australian National Botanic Gardens]] | url = http://www.anbg.gov.au/stamps/garden-a-2000.html | access-date = 27 February 2007 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20060831225854/http://anbg.gov.au/stamps/garden-a-2000.html | archive-date = 31 August 2006}}</ref>
